source_text: XXXIII. Atque ut viri illi Doctissimi mentem suam ea de re distinctius explicent, aiunt, Se considerare in objecto scientiae divinae duos status, possibilitatis & futuritionis, sed tria momenta. Primum, quando Deus intuendo suam omnipotentiam vidit quid absque contradictione a se fieri possit. Alterum, quando omnium fieri possibilium modos, connexiones, & concatenationes apud se decreto absoluto praefinivit, id est, quid causa, quid effectum, quid medium, quid finis, quid prius, quid simul, quid posterius foret, aut non foret; Sed cum hac cautione, si vellet eas futuras. Tertium, quando inter illas res, sub conditione tali praefinitas, discrimen statuit, relicta quibusdam conditione illa, & superaddito tali decreto, Nolo futuras, ab aliis sublata conditione, ejusque in locum substituto tali decreto, Volo futuras. In tertio momento, rem demum extrahi ex statu possibilitatis in statum futuritionis: in prioribus duobus manere in statu possibilitatis; hoc tamen discrimine, quod eas in primo per naturam, & ante omnem voluntatis actum cognoscat, in secundo post actum voluntatis. Quae sunt quoque eorum verba tertia illa sectione, num. 13. Ex quibus verbis patet eos futura contingentia sub conditione non habere pro vere futuris, sed pro mere possibilibus, & tamen velle ut eorum cognitio, non ad scientiam Dei naturalem, sed ad liberam pertineat.
english: To set out their view on the matter more distinctly, those very learned men say that in the object of God's knowledge they consider two states, possibility and futurity, but three moments. In the first, God, looking at his own omnipotence, saw what he could do without contradiction. In the second, by an absolute decree he fixed beforehand within himself the modes, connections and sequences of everything that could be made: what would or would not be cause, effect, means and end, what would come before, together or after. He did this with one proviso: if he willed them to be future.

In the third, among the things fixed beforehand under that condition, he made a distinction. For some he left the condition standing and added the decree 'I do not will them to be future.' For others he removed the condition and put in its place the decree 'I will them to be future.'

Only in the third moment, they say, is a thing finally brought out of the state of possibility into the state of futurity. In the first two it stays in the state of possibility. The difference is that God knows things in the first moment by nature, before any act of his will, and in the second after an act of his will. These too are their words, in that third section, number 13.

Their words make it plain that they treat contingent futures under a condition not as truly future but as merely possible. Yet they want the knowledge of them to belong not to God's natural knowledge but to his free knowledge.

source_text: XXXIV. Porro hanc suam doctrinam fatentur illi se sumpsisse a Samuele Retorforti Scoto, ex quo, ut certissimum fundamentum, ibidem supponunt: Quod voluntas Dei ad nulla entia, vel quae actu sunt, vel quae sunt in potentia, seu aliquando actuanda, seu in actum nunquam deducenda, sit indeterminata, dubia, aut suspensa, seu habens in se potentialitatem, suspensionem & privationem actus secundi, qualis reperitur in voluntate creata, sed quod sit per eminentiam sui actus, respectu omnis entis ab aeterno determinata. Unde colligunt, Deum necessario velle, vel non velle omnes concatenationes & connexiones entium possibiles, adeoque in omnibus propositionibus conditionatis de futuro contingenti, verum esse ex definita & certa Dei voluntate, quod si talis vel talis conditio poneretur, sequeretur hoc & non aliud.
english: They admit that they took this doctrine from the Scot Samuel Rutherford, and in the same place they lay down, as a most certain foundation drawn from him, the following. God's will is not undetermined, doubtful or suspended toward any being, whether actual or potential, and whether it is to be actualized at some time or never brought into act.
Nor does his will contain potentiality, suspension and the lack of a second act, as a created will does. By the eminence of its act it is determined from eternity with respect to every being.

From this they infer that God necessarily wills or does not will every possible sequence and connection of beings. So in every conditional proposition about a contingent future, it is true by God's definite and certain will that if this or that condition were in place, this and nothing else would follow.

source_text: XXXV. Et certe Retorfortis ille, nuper in Academia Andreapolitana, Theologiae Professor, Vir quoque Doctus & subtilis, eodem utens principio, affirmat Keilitas Davidem in manus Saulis tradituros, si apud eos permansisset, & Tyrios acturos poenitentiam, si signa vidissent, & alia ejusmodi, Deus cognovit scientia libera in decreto praedeterminante, quo concatenationem entium omnium possibilium absolute praedefinivit, quod certe, inquit, spectat ad admirandam Dei providentiam, cujus voluntas ad nulla entia, vel quae actu sunt, vel quae possibilia sunt, est indeterminata & suspensa. In Exercitationibus Apologeticis pro divina gratia, cap. 5. de scientia Media.
english: Rutherford himself, lately professor of theology at the University of St Andrews, also a learned and subtle man, uses the same principle. He states that God knew by free knowledge, in a predetermining decree, that the people of Keilah would hand David over to Saul if he had stayed with them, that the Tyrians would have repented if they had seen the signs, and other things of the kind.

By that decree, he says, God absolutely fixed beforehand the sequence of all possible beings. 'This certainly,' he says, 'belongs to the wonderful providence of God, whose will is undetermined and suspended toward no beings, whether actual or possible.' Exercitationes Apologeticae pro Divina Gratia, chapter 5, on middle knowledge.

source_text: XXXVI. Alii vero existimant, multas aut innumeras potius propositiones de futuris contingentibus sub aliqua conditione fieri & fingi posse, quae sub scientiam divinam non cadunt, nec quicquam exprimunt quod ab ipso Deo sciri & cognosci possit, non quod Deum veritatem ullam ignorare, aut aliquid esse revera futurum quod Deus futurum non sciat, sed quoniam existimant propositiones istas nihil significare quod determinate verum vel falsum sit; & quae in eis futura sub certa conditione negantur, vel affirmantur, non esse magis futura, quam non futura, sed indifferentia ad utrumque.
english: Others, however, think that many, or rather countless, propositions about contingent futures under some condition can be framed and made up that do not fall under God's knowledge. They express nothing that God himself can know or understand.

This is not because God is ignorant of any truth, or because something is really future that God does not know to be future. It is because, in their view, such propositions signify nothing that is determinately true or false. What they affirm or deny as future under a certain condition is no more future than not future; it is open either way.

source_text: XXXVII. Exempli causa, affirmat aliquis, quod si Deus mundum alium crearet, & certos Angelos in eo conderet, in his, aut illis circumstantiis, Angeli isti essent in officio suo & amore Dei perseveraturi. Ex eorum mente, id quod affirmatur in conditionali ista propositione neque verum, neque falsum est, ac proinde ut tale a Deo cognosci non potest; sed res est ex se mere possibilis, & quae indifferens est, ut ita sit, vel non sit; Eamque ita se habere novit Deus; ac proinde, si dicatur ista propositione nullam veritatem Deo scibilem contineri, omniscientiae divinae nihil propterea detrahitur.
english: Suppose someone says that if God created another world and placed certain angels in it in these or those circumstances, those angels would persevere in their duty and in the love of God. On their view, what that conditional proposition asserts is neither true nor false, and so God cannot know it as true or false.

The matter is of itself merely possible and open to being so or not being so, and God knows that this is how it stands. So if it is said that the proposition contains no truth God can know, God's omniscience loses nothing.

source_text: XXXVIII. Etenim absurdam putant sententiam eorum qui infinita decreta Deo tribuunt de connexionibus contingentibus cujuscunque possibilis cum altero possibili, etiam in iis in quibus nullus ordo, subordinatio, aut cohaerentia apparet. Quasi Deus decrevisset quaecunque futura essent in infinitis mundis a se creabilibus, suppositis infinitis diversis conditionibus. Quae est sententia jamjam ex Samuele Retorforti, & Thesibus Voetii relata: quam expresse rejicit Strangius, Tractatu de Voluntate & Actionibus Dei circa peccatum, lib. 1. cap. 5. & lib. 3. cap. 13. Et Tuissus quoque in dissertatione de scientia Media, lib. 3. pag. 472.
english: They consider absurd the view of those who ascribe to God countless decrees about contingent connections between any one possible thing and another. This includes cases where no order, subordination or coherence appears. It is as though God had decreed whatever would happen in the countless worlds he could create, under countless different conditions.

This is the view just reported from Samuel Rutherford and from Voetius's theses. William Strang expressly rejects it in his treatise On the Will and Actions of God concerning Sin, book 1, chapter 5, and book 3, chapter 13. So does Twisse in his dissertation on middle knowledge, book 3, page 472.

source_text: XXXIX. Neque tamen negant omnem in Deo scientiam eorum quae essent, vel fuissent contingenter futura, sub aliqua conditione, quae nunquam posita est, nec etiam unquam ponenda. Agnoscunt enim ejusmodi quaedam in scriptura praedici, adeoque Deo nota & perspecta fuisse. Sed pertendunt istam scientiam non praecessisse liberum voluntatis divinae decretum. Non quod admittant in Deo decreta quaedam conditionata, quibus velit aliquid fieri sub conditione quae nunquam locum habitura est: aut etiam explicita & formalia decreta de connexione duorum eventuum quorum neutrum revera existet: sed quoniam ex absolutis quibusdam Dei decretis de rebus reapse futuris sequitur, posita tali, vel tali conditione, haec & illa futura fuisse.
english: Even so, they do not deny that God has any knowledge of things that would be or would have been contingently future under a condition that has never been, and never will be, fulfilled. They grant that some things of this kind are foretold in Scripture and so were known to God and clearly seen by him. What they insist on is that this knowledge did not come before the free decree of God's will.

This is not because they allow in God conditional decrees, by which he wills something to happen under a condition that will never obtain. Nor do they allow explicit, formal decrees about the connection of two events, neither of which will actually exist. Their reason is that, given this or that condition, it follows from certain absolute decrees of God about things that will really happen that these or those things would have come about.

source_text: XL. Exempli causa, noverat Deus Saulem venturum in urbem Kehilam, & Kehilanos Davidem Sauli tradituros, si David ea in urbe maneret: quia decreverat Davidem ex manibus Saulis eripere, non per miraculum aliquod, aut extraordinariam quandam animi mutationem sive in Saule, sive in Kehilanis, sed per Davidis recessum & fugam; Unde sequitur Davidem in manus Saulis fuisse tradendum si mansisset apud Kehilanos: quanquam explicitum ejusmodi decretum in Deo non ponamus, Volo ut Ceilani Davidem tradant si maneat apud ipsos.
english: For example, God knew that Saul would come to the city of Keilah and that its people would hand David over to Saul if David stayed there. He knew it because he had decreed to rescue David from Saul's hands not by a miracle or by some extraordinary change of heart in Saul or in the people of Keilah, but by David's withdrawal and flight.

It follows that David would have been handed over to Saul if he had stayed with the people of Keilah. Yet we do not posit in God an explicit decree of the form 'I will that the people of Keilah hand David over if he stays with them.'

source_text: XLI. Sic rem istam exponit Guil. Amesius in sua rescriptione ad Grevinchovii Responsum cap. 15. Dignum, inquit, & hoc accurata contemplatione: decretum Dei vel ut formale statutum & explicitum concipi, vel ut implicitum & virtuale, quod virtute alterius decreti includitur: implicitum vero tantum dari in futuris conditionatis contingentibus, quae nunquam existunt, quia virtute actuali decretis, hoc vel illo posito existerent. Decreverat Deus liberare Davidem a manibus virorum Ceilae mediante fuga, non mutatione animorum praeter ordinem. Ex hoc actuali fluit conditionatum illud contingens: si non fugiat David, tradetur. Et hoc sensu ait futurum conditionatum decreto libero inniti, adeoque per Visionis scientiam intelligi, quae non sit de iis tantum quae absolute futura sunt; sed & de iis quae ex actuali decreto jam facto fluerent, hac vel illa conditione posita.
english: William Ames explains the matter this way in his rescript to Grevinchoven's Response, chapter 15. 'This too,' he says, 'deserves careful consideration. A decree of God may be conceived either as a formal and explicit statute, or as implicit and virtual, contained by the force of another decree. Only the implicit kind applies to conditional contingent futures that never come to exist, because by the force of actual decrees they would exist if this or that were posited.

God had decreed to free David from the men of Keilah by means of flight, not by changing their minds outside the usual order. From this actual decree flows the conditional contingent: if David does not flee, he will be handed over.'

In this sense, Ames says, the conditional future rests on the free decree and so is understood by the knowledge of vision. That knowledge covers not only what will absolutely happen, but also what would flow from an actual decree already made, given this or that condition.

source_text: XLII. Porro praecipuum fundamentum quo nituntur Tuissus, Retorfortis, Voetius, Amesius, & alii, dum negant in Deo dari cognitionem contingenter futurorum sub aliqua conditione, ante liberum ipsius decretum, illud est quod, ex eorum mente, Nihil futurum est priusquam decreverit Deus illud esse futurum. Unde sequitur, ante Dei decretum nihil ut futurum concipi atque cognosci posse. Nihil autem vel absolute vel conditionate futurum esse, priusquam decernat Deus illud esse futurum, inde probant, quod nulla causa fingi vel cogitari possit, per quam res ex possibili ab aeterno futura fiat, praeter Dei decretum. Cum enim nihil temporale causa possit esse ejus quod aeternum est, ad nihil eorum quae in tempore fiunt, futuritionis, quae est ab aeterno, causa referri debet, sed necesse est ut ista futuritio causam habeat aliquam aeternam, quae alia esse non potest quam liberum Dei decretum: ut millies repetit Tuissus in sua dissertatione de scientia Media.
english: Twisse, Rutherford, Voetius, Ames and others deny that God knows, before his free decree, what would contingently happen under some condition. The main foundation they rely on is that, on their view, nothing is future until God has decreed that it shall be. It follows that before God's decree nothing can be conceived or known as future.

They prove that nothing is future, absolutely or conditionally, before God decrees it, on these grounds. No cause can be imagined or thought of, other than God's decree, by which a thing passes from being possible to being future from eternity. Nothing temporal can cause what is eternal.

So the futurity that exists from eternity cannot be traced to anything that happens in time. It must have some eternal cause, and that can only be God's free decree. Twisse repeats this a thousand times in his dissertation on middle knowledge.

source_text: XLIII. Voetius vero, seu apud ipsum Nathenus, postquam multis disputavit contra scientiam Mediam, sic tandem concludit, Ex iis quae hactenus contra scientiam mediam disputata sunt, manifestum est totam praesentis controversiae difficultatem recidere in hoc punctum: An futura conditionata libera, ex sua natura ad futuritionem & non futuritionem indifferentia, ab aeterno potuerint transiisse in statum rei futurae aliter quam per decretum divinum, quod causa sit omnis qualiscunque etiam futuritionis? Hoc est fundamentum fundamentorum, cui tota causae moles incumbit; hoc est postulatum illud quod & nos adversariis concedere, & ipsi nobis probare non possunt.
english: Voetius, or rather Nethenus in Voetius's work, after arguing at length against middle knowledge, finally concludes: 'From what has been argued so far against middle knowledge, it is clear that the whole difficulty of the present controversy comes down to this point.

Could free conditional futures, which by their own nature are open to being future or not future, have passed from eternity into the state of something future in any way other than by the divine decree, which is the cause of every kind of futurity whatever? This is the foundation of foundations, on which the whole weight of the case rests. It is the postulate that we cannot grant our opponents and they cannot prove to us.'

source_text: XLIV. Strangius vero qui non putat, cum modo dictis Theologis, cujuslibet eventus ab aeterno futuritionem non aliunde quam ex Dei libero decreto pendere, alio argumento, quod invictum esse existimat, probare contendit contingentia libera, ut futura non posse a Deo cognosci, ex ulla hypothesi, ex qua non necessario inferatur determinatio voluntatis creatae. Argumentum autem ejus tale est. Conditionata quorum consequens non habet necessariam connexionem cum antecedente non possunt certo sciri, ac proinde nec sunt scibilia a Deo, cujus scientia est certissima & omnino infallibilis. At ejusmodi sunt conditionata quae statuuntur esse objectum scientiae mediae, &c. Majorem probat, quia, inquit, Nisi objectum sit certo verum, certo cognosci non potest: quamdiu enim res est incerta, certo sciri non potest; nihil autem est certo verum quod non est necessario verum, necessario inquam vel absolute, vel ex hypothesi. Ac proinde conditionata scientia ut sit certa & infallibilis, oportet ut objectum ejus sit conditionata propositio necessaria: nulla autem conditionalis propositio est necessaria, in qua illatio non est necessaria. Tractatu de Voluntate Dei circa peccatum lib. 3. cap. 11.
english: Strang does not agree with the theologians just named that the futurity of every event from eternity depends on nothing but God's free decree. He tries to prove by another argument, which he considers unanswerable, that God cannot know free contingents as future on any supposition from which the determination of the created will does not necessarily follow.

His argument runs like this. Conditionals whose consequent has no necessary connection with the antecedent cannot be known with certainty, and so God cannot know them either, since his knowledge is entirely certain and infallible. The conditionals said to be the object of middle knowledge are of this kind, and so on.

He proves the major premise as follows: 'Unless the object is certainly true, it cannot be known with certainty. As long as the matter is uncertain, it cannot be known with certainty. But nothing is certainly true that is not necessarily true, necessarily, I mean, either absolutely or on a hypothesis.

So for conditional knowledge to be certain and infallible, its object must be a necessary conditional proposition. And no conditional proposition is necessary unless the inference in it is necessary.' Treatise on the Will of God concerning Sin, book 3, chapter 11.

source_text: XLV. Ut autem quid ipse quoque sentio paucis aperiam, Primo illud certum est &, ut patet ex dictis, ab omnibus concessum, Nihil esse sub ulla conditione libere futurum, & ut tale cognosci posse, nisi in conditione sub qua futurum dicitur, includatur Dei decretum de non denegando creaturae concursu ad agendum necessario. Nempe propositiones omnes de futuris conditionatis, ut verae esse possint, sic exponendae & intelligendae sunt; creatura haec, vel illa in tali rerum ordine constituta, hoc aut illud faciet; modo Deus velit cum ea concurrere, prout concurrere solet, & ut concurrat necesse est ad hoc ut creatura actionem suam elicere possit.
english: To state briefly what I myself think: first, it is certain and, as is clear from what has been said, granted by everyone, that nothing is freely future under any condition, or can be known as such, unless God's decree not to deny the creature the concurrence necessary for acting is included in the condition under which it is said to be future.

That is, if any proposition about conditional futures is to be capable of truth, it must be explained and understood like this: this or that creature, placed in such an order of things, will do this or that, provided God wills to concur with it as he usually does. He must concur if the creature is to be able to put forth its action.

source_text: XLVI. Secundo, illud quoque concedendum existimo, propositiones omnes de futuris conditionatis liberis & contingentibus, in quibus ejusmodi conditio subintelligitur, determinate veras vel falsas esse. Saltem hoc negare non possunt Thomistae recentiores, & alii qui cum ipsis in hoc negotio sentiunt, & alioqui scientiam Mediam acerrime impugnant. Cum enim ad hoc ut creatura agat, ex eorum sententia, necesse sit Deum illam praemovere & praedeterminare, posita autem Dei praedeterminatione, necessario sequatur creaturae actio, juxta eorum hypotheses infallibilis & necessaria est haec conditionalis, Si Deus vellet talem creaturam in hoc, aut illo statu constituere, & nihil ad agendum necessarium ipsi denegare, hoc aut illud ageret: quandoquidem in illa conditione continetur decretum Dei de illa ad agendum praedeterminanda.
english: Second, I think it must also be granted that every proposition about free and contingent conditional futures, where a condition of that kind is understood, is determinately true or false. At any rate the later Thomists cannot deny this, nor can others who agree with them on this matter while otherwise attacking middle knowledge fiercely.

On their view, for a creature to act God must premove and predetermine it, and once God's predetermination is posited the creature's action follows necessarily. So on their assumptions this conditional is infallible and necessary: if God willed to place such a creature in this or that state and to deny it nothing it needs to act, it would do this or that. For that condition contains God's decree to predetermine the creature to act.

source_text: XLVII. Et certe quae rationes suadent absolutas propositiones de futuris contingentibus determinatam veritatem, vel falsitatem habere, in hisce conditionatis locum etiam habere videntur. Nempe quod fieri non potest, quin ex duabus contradictoriis, altera sit vera, altera falsa. Item quod in omni disjunctiva vera, una pars saltem debet esse vera. Nam haec disjunctiva vera est, Si Petrus in occasione tali constituatur, nec Deus ei solitum concursum suum deneget, peccabit, vel non peccabit. Et hae quoque duae sibi mutuo contradicunt, Petrus si in eo rerum ordine collocetur, nec Deus nolit cum eo ad agendum concurrere, hoc aget. Et Petrus si in eo rerum ordine collocetur, nec Deus nolit cum eo ad agendum concurrere, hoc non aget.
english: The reasons that lead us to hold that absolute propositions about contingent futures are determinately true or false seem to apply to these conditionals as well. One is that of two contradictories one must be true and the other false. Another is that in every true disjunction at least one part must be true.

For this disjunction is true: if Peter is placed in such an occasion and God does not deny him his usual concurrence, he will sin or he will not sin. These two propositions also contradict each other: 'If Peter is placed in that order of things and God is not unwilling to concur with him in acting, he will do this,' and 'If Peter is placed in that order of things and God is not unwilling to concur with him in acting, he will not do this.'

source_text: XLVIII. Quod si quis dicat nihil futurum esse, nisi dependenter a Dei decreto; & sic ante decretum Dei, rem non esse magis futuram quam non futuram, sed indifferentem ad hoc, ut futura vel non futura sit; adeoque neutrum de ea vere affirmari posse: Respondeo ad hoc, ut res absolute futura sit, praerequiri quidem quoddam Dei decretum, a quo pendeat ejus futuritio: sed ad hoc ut res non sit simpliciter futura, sed tantum futura esset sub aliqua conditione, non requiri decretum quod actu in Deo sit; sed sufficere decretum quod, juxta hypothesin, in Deo ponendum esset.
english: Someone may object that nothing is future except in dependence on God's decree. Before God's decree, then, a thing is no more future than not future, but open to being either, so that neither can truly be said of it.

My answer is this. For a thing to be absolutely future, some decree of God on which its futurity depends is indeed required beforehand. But for a thing not to be simply future, only future under some condition, no decree actually present in God is needed. It is enough that there be a decree that would have to be posited in God on that hypothesis.

source_text: XLIX. Praeterea certum est, & ab omnibus concessum, nullam omnino veritatem qualiscunque sit fugere intellectum divinum: ac proinde cum propositiones de libere futuris, sub conditione saepius exposita, determinatam veritatem habeant, sunt illae quoque divinae scientiae objectum. Adeoque novit Deus quid singulae creaturae possibiles facturae essent, si vellet illas in hoc aut illo statu condere, nec eis quicquam negare eorum quae ad agendum necessaria sunt.
english: Again, it is certain and granted by all that no truth whatever escapes God's intellect. Propositions about free futures, under the condition explained more than once, have determinate truth, so they too are objects of God's knowledge.
God therefore knows what every possible creature would do if he willed to establish it in this or that state and to deny it nothing it needs in order to act.

source_text: L. Hanc etiam propositionem, quae ex praecedenti sequitur, negare non possunt illi qui sine Dei concursu praevio & praedeterminante, nullam a creaturis actionem edi posse putant. Manifestum est enim, fieri non posse quin Deus cognoscat, quid acturae essent singulae creaturae possibiles, si vellet eas non tantum creare, sed etiam ad agendum applicare & praedeterminare. Istud fatetur Tuissus, qui postquam observavit Suarezium docere propositiones conditionatas de futuris contingentibus, quae sunt objectum scientiae divinae, includere in antecedente voluntatem divinam, scilicet, si ipsa velit talem effectum, vel saltem velit illum permittere, & ad illum concurrere, subjungit, Juxta hunc sensum concedimus conditionales illas obtinere quas fingunt Jesuitae. Dissertatione de scientia Media, lib. 3. pag. 465.
english: Those who hold that creatures can perform no action without God's prior, predetermining concurrence cannot deny this proposition either, which follows from the one before. Plainly God cannot fail to know what each possible creature would do if he willed not only to create it but also to apply it to act and predetermine it.

Twisse admits as much. He notes that Suarez teaches that the conditional propositions about contingent futures that are the object of God's knowledge include God's will in the antecedent: that is, if God himself willed such an effect, or at least willed to permit it and to concur with it. Twisse then adds: 'In this sense we grant that the conditionals the Jesuits invent do hold.' Dissertation on middle knowledge, book 3, page 465.

source_text: LI. Nec minus evidens est, juxta eorundem Doctorum principia, scientiam illam qua Deus cognoscit quid creatura quaelibet possibilis actura esset in hoc aut illo rerum statu, si Deus illi concursum ad agendum necessarium subministrare vellet, in Deo locum habere ratione priusquam de rebus quicquam decreverit. Etenim priusquam concipiamus Deum aliquid decernere, verum est, quod si Deus creaturam aliquam vellet concursu suo ad agendum movere & praedeterminare, ageret proculdubio id ad quod moveretur & determinaretur. Nec veritas hujus propositionis ab aliquo Dei decreto antecedente pendet, quo decreta sit connexio possibilis illius decreti cum eventu qui ex illo sequeretur.
english: It is just as clear, on the principles of those same teachers, that the knowledge by which God knows what any possible creature would do in this or that state of things, if he willed to supply it with the concurrence it needs to act, exists in God prior in the order of reason to any decree of his about things.

Before we conceive of God decreeing anything, it is true that if God willed to move and predetermine some creature to act by his concurrence, it would certainly do what it was moved and determined to do. The truth of this proposition does not depend on some earlier decree of God fixing the connection between that possible decree and the event that would follow from it.

source_text: LII. Imo etiam plane commentitium, neque tantum sapientiae, sed etiam divinae bonitati repugnans videtur illud decretum quo nonnulli volunt, ut supra retulimus, Deum omnium fieri possibilium connexiones & concatenationes apud se praefinivisse, priusquam decerneret aliquid esse futurum. Nam si ita esset, oporteret ut Deus, antequam hunc mundum creare statueret, hujusmodi decreta apud se concepisset, si velim Adamum creare, volo ut ejus lapsus cum ejus tentatione necessario cohaereat. Si velim creare Davidem & illum videre Bathscebah, volo ut cum isto visu connexa sit istius mulieris concupiscentia. Item, volo ut tales occasiones peccandi consequantur talia peccata, si decernam tales occasiones fore. Imo volo ut in infinitis mundis a me creabilibus hi & illi eventus contingenter possibiles cum his & illis ejusdem naturae eventibus nexum habeant inseparabilem. Quae certe decreta non tantum plane otiosa, frivola & frustranea sunt, sed maxime dedecent bonitatem & justitiam illius qui Deus nolens iniquitatem est.
english: Indeed, the decree some posit, as reported above, by which God fixed within himself the connections and sequences of everything that could be made before he decreed anything to be future, seems pure invention. It seems contrary not only to God's wisdom but also to his goodness.

If it were so, God would have had to form decrees like these within himself before resolving to create this world: 'If I will to create Adam, I will that his fall be necessarily bound up with his temptation. If I will to create David and that he see Bathsheba, I will that lust for that woman be joined to that sight.'

Or again: 'I will that such occasions of sin be followed by such sins, if I decree that such occasions shall exist.' Or even: 'I will that in the countless worlds I could create, these or those contingently possible events be inseparably linked with these or those events of the same kind.'
Such decrees are not only plainly idle, trivial and pointless. They are utterly unworthy of the goodness and justice of the one who is a God who does not will iniquity.

source_text: LIII. Negari ergo cum aliqua ratione non potest, & debet ab omnibus concedi, dari in Deo scientiam quandam eorum quae libere & contingenter futura sunt, sub certa conditione, antequam ullum actuale de rebus futuris decretum in Deo concipiamus. Tota difficultas est An conditio sub qua res futura dicitur, includere debeat decretum de causa secunda ad agendum praemovenda ac praedeterminanda, an vero sufficiat ut decretum, quod juxta conditionem illam in Deo ponendum esset, sit solum de praebendo concursu quodam ex se indifferenti, & qui a causa secunda ad certam actionis speciem determinetur.
english: So it cannot reasonably be denied, and everyone ought to grant, that God has a certain knowledge of what is freely and contingently future under a certain condition, before we conceive of any actual decree in God about future things.

The whole difficulty is this. Must the condition under which something is said to be future include a decree to premove and predetermine the second cause to act? Or is it enough that the decree which that condition would require in God be simply a decree to provide a concurrence that is of itself indifferent and is determined by the second cause to a particular kind of action?

source_text: LIV. Omnes illi Theologi qui sine concursu Dei causam secundam ad agendum applicante & praedeterminante nihil fieri existimant, pertendunt nullam propositionem de futuris contingentibus & conditionatis veritatem aliquam habere, adeoque ut veram esse cognoscibilem, nisi in conditione supponatur decretum de agente libero praemovendo & praedeterminando. Volunt enim actionis cujuscunque futuritionem a tali decreto pendere, imo juxta nonnullos, tanquam a causa unica atque solitaria, & sine tali decreto nullam causae secundae actionem futuram esse posse. Verum in ea sumus sententia causas secundas multa in tempore agere ad quae a Deo non praedeterminantur. Nec enim videmus quomodo Deus autor peccati non esset, si praedeterminaret causas liberas ad actus per se vitiosos & intrinsece malos, verbi causa ad blasphemiam, & ad Dei odium. Si autem actio aliqua causae liberae esse potest sine Dei praemotione & praedeterminatione, ad hoc ut actio aliqua futura sit, vel futura esset, non necesse est poni, vel supponi in Deo decretum de creatura ad agendum praemovenda & praedeterminanda: sed sufficit decretum de eo concursu praebendo, sine quo creatura nihil agere potest, & qui ad ejus actionem revera necessarius est.
english: All the theologians who think nothing happens without God's concurrence applying and predetermining the second cause to act insist that no proposition about contingent conditional futures has any truth, or can be known as true, unless a decree to premove and predetermine the free agent is assumed in the condition.
They hold that the futurity of every action depends on such a decree, and some even make it the sole and only cause. Without such a decree, they say, no action of a second cause can be future.

Our view, however, is that second causes do many things in time to which God does not predetermine them. We do not see how God would escape being the author of sin if he predetermined free causes to acts that are vicious in themselves and intrinsically evil, such as blasphemy and hatred of God.

But if a free cause can perform some action without God's premotion and predetermination, then for an action to be future, or to be such that it would be future, there is no need to posit or suppose in God a decree to premove and predetermine the creature to act. A decree to provide the concurrence without which the creature can do nothing, and which its action really needs, is enough.

source_text: LV. Praesertim vero illud nullo modo probare possum quod Gul. Tuissus pluribus in locis asserit, decretum Dei & ejus voluntatem esse solam & unicam causam futuritionis cujuslibet eventus. Quid enim, An Dei decretum sola causa est cur Adam inobediens Deo futurus fuit: Et similiter cur Angeli illi qui ceciderunt, fuerunt adversus Deum superbia sese elaturi? Quis hoc dicentem audire sustineat? aut hoc dicere possit quin Deum peccati authorem manifeste faciat?
english: Above all, I cannot accept in any way what William Twisse asserts in many places: that God's decree and will is the one and only cause of the futurity of every event.

What then? Is God's decree the only reason why Adam was going to disobey God, and likewise why the angels who fell were going to exalt themselves against God in pride? Who could bear to hear anyone say so? Or who could say it without plainly making God the author of sin?

source_text: LVI. At, inquit, Doctus ille vir, futuritionis quae ab aeterno fuit nulla causa dari potest quae ab aeterno non fuerit. Nihil enim temporale causa est ejus quod ab aeterno est. Sed nihil ab aeterno fuit praeter Deum ipsum, qui non nisi per liberam suam voluntatem ad extra operatur. Respondeo, argumentum istud supponit futuritionem esse aliquid reale a re ipsa futura distinctum, & quod causam aliam habeat quam res ipsa futura. At hoc falsissimum est. Nam futuritio nihil aliud est quam respectus quidam rationis, & extrinseca denominatio rei quae futura dicitur: non vero ens aliquod a re futura distinctum, & quod requirat causam quandam diversam ab ipsius rei futurae causa. Et hoc patet ex ipso argumento. Nam recte ponit argumentum ab aeterno nihil fuisse praeter Deum: ac proinde futuritio quae ab aeterno fuisse dicitur, vel nihil reale fuit, vel fuit ipse Deus.
english: 'But,' says that learned man, 'no cause can be given for a futurity that existed from eternity unless the cause itself existed from eternity. Nothing temporal causes what exists from eternity. But nothing existed from eternity except God himself, who acts outside himself only through his free will.'

My answer is that this argument assumes that futurity is something real, distinct from the future thing itself and having a cause other than that thing. That is entirely false. Futurity is nothing but a certain relation of reason, an extrinsic denomination of the thing said to be future. It is not some being distinct from the future thing that needs a cause different from the cause of the future thing itself.
The argument itself makes this plain. It rightly assumes that nothing existed from eternity except God. So the futurity said to have existed from eternity was either nothing real or God himself.

source_text: LVII. Igitur quod est causa cur res in tempore aliquando existat, idem plane causa est cur res ab aeterno extitura fuerit. Sicut quod causa est cur res aliquando fuit, causa est cur in aeternum dicetur praeterita. Nec magis requiritur causa ab aeterno existens, ut res ab aeterno futura fuerit, quam requiritur causa in aeternum duratura, ut in aeternum res praeterita sit. Ad effectum futurum sufficit causa futura, sicut ad praeteritum sufficit causa praeterita.
english: So whatever causes a thing to exist at some point in time is exactly what causes it to have been going to exist from eternity. In the same way, whatever is the cause of a thing's having been at some time is the cause of its being called past for ever.

A cause existing from eternity is no more needed for a thing to have been future from eternity than a cause lasting for ever is needed for a thing to be past for ever. A future cause is enough for a future effect, just as a past cause is enough for a past one.

source_text: LVIII. Cum ergo Deus in tempore causa peccati non sit, tantum abest ut dicendum putem Dei voluntatem esse causam unicam futuritionis peccati, ut plane & simpliciter negandum existimem illam esse istius futuritionis causam, vel solam, vel cum causa secunda. Verum est quidem hominem non peccare, nisi dependenter a Dei voluntate. Nec enim peccare posset, nisi Deus ipsum peccare permitteret. Et sic quoque peccati futuritio pendet a decreto Dei de peccato permittendo. Sed quemadmodum Dei voluntas non propterea dicenda est propria causa cur homo actu peccet; sic etiam inde non sequitur Dei decretum esse propriam causam futuritionis peccati.
english: Since God is not the cause of sin in time, I am far from thinking we should say that God's will is the only cause of sin's futurity. On the contrary, I judge that we must deny plainly and without qualification that it is the cause of that futurity at all, whether on its own or together with the second cause.
It is true that man sins only in dependence on God's will, since he could not sin unless God permitted him to. In that sense the futurity of sin also depends on God's decree to permit sin.
But God's will is not for that reason to be called the proper cause of man's actually sinning. In the same way, it does not follow that God's decree is the proper cause of the futurity of sin.

source_text: LIX. Sed etiam nonnulli eorum qui statuunt quosdam actus liberos absolute esse futuros, & ut tales a Deo praesciri, absque ullo decreto causas liberas ad istos actus praedeterminandi, ut Doctissimus Strangius; negant tamen futura contingentia libera a Deo cognosci posse ex ulla hypothesi quae non infert necessario determinationem voluntatis creatae, & proinde quae non includit absolutum decretum de eorum futuritione. Ut apud eundem Strangium videre est de Voluntate Dei circa peccatum, lib. 3. cap. 11.
english: Even some who hold that certain free acts are absolutely future, and are foreknown as such by God without any decree predetermining free causes to those acts, still deny that God can know free contingent futures on any supposition that does not necessarily entail the determination of the created will, and so does not include an absolute decree that these acts shall be future. The very learned Strang is one of them.
This can be seen in Strang himself, On the Will of God concerning Sin, book 3, chapter 11.

source_text: LX. Ratio autem ejus est, ut supra retulimus, quod nihil certo cognosci potest quod non sit certo verum: nihil autem certo verum est quod necessarium non sit vel absolute, vel ex hypothesi. Unde colligit futura conditionata non posse esse objectum scientiae divinae, quae infallibilis & certissima est, nisi in conditione includatur aliquid unde quod dicitur futurum necessario inferatur. Sed si haec ratio valeret, nullum contingens Deus praescire posset tanquam absolute futurum, nisi quod prius absolute futurum decrevisset: quod tamen non admittit Strangius, qui fatetur homines multa libere agere ad quae a Deo non praedeterminantur.
english: His reason, as reported above, is that nothing can be known with certainty that is not certainly true, and nothing is certainly true that is not necessary either absolutely or on a hypothesis. He concludes that conditional futures cannot be the object of God's knowledge, which is infallible and entirely certain, unless the condition includes something from which what is called future follows necessarily.

But if this argument held, God could foreknow no contingent thing as absolutely future except what he had first decreed to be absolutely future. Yet Strang does not accept that, since he grants that people freely do many things to which God does not predetermine them.

source_text: LXI. Sed, ait vir ille Doctus, quicquid Deus praevidet ut absolute futurum, quantumlibet in se contingens sit, & simpliciter loquendo possit non esse, necessarium est tamen ex hypothesi, non quidem ex hypothesi divini alicujus decreti praedeterminantis, sed ex hac illa ipsa hypothesi quod futurum est. Etenim quemadmodum quicquid est, dum est, necessario est; ita etiam quicquid futurum est, hoc ipso quod supponitur futurum, necessario futurum est, & sic a Deo certo cognosci potest.
english: 'But,' says that learned man, 'whatever God foresees as absolutely future, however contingent it may be in itself and able, strictly speaking, not to be, is still necessary on a hypothesis. The hypothesis is not some divine predetermining decree, but simply that it is future.
Just as whatever is, is necessarily while it is, so whatever is future, by the very fact that it is assumed to be future, is necessarily future. And so God can know it with certainty.'

source_text: LXII. Sed quod vir Doctissimus de absolute futuris dicendum existimat, non minori cum ratione ad conditionate futura applicari potest. Dicam enim eodem modo Deum certo praevidere quod libere futurum esset sub aliqua conditione; quia licet causa libera posset aliter agere, nec ista conditio illi necessitatem agendi imponeret, nihilominus reipsa sic ageret. Ex hypothesi autem quod sic ageret, necesse est ut sic agat posita conditione, & ita res est quae possit a Deo certo sciri.
english: What that very learned man thinks must be said of absolute futures can be applied with no less reason to conditional futures. I will say in the same way that God foresees with certainty what would freely happen under some condition.

He foresees it because, although the free cause could act otherwise and the condition would not force it to act, it would in fact act in this way. On the hypothesis that it would act in this way, it must act so once the condition is in place. So it is something God can know with certainty.

source_text: LXIII. Nihil ergo video cur negemus Deo scientiam eorum quae libere futura essent sub certa conditione, quanquam in conditione ista non includatur decretum de causa libera ad hoc vel illud praedeterminanda. Et si quae argumenta scientiam istam videntur evertere, ut quod capi non potest qua ratione Deus infallibiliter cognoscat futurum esse quod posset non esse, pugnant illa quoque cum praescientia contingentium quae sunt absolute futura; quam tamen in Deo dari verbum Dei ponit extra omne dubium.
english: I therefore see no reason to deny God knowledge of what would freely happen under a certain condition, even though the condition does not include a decree predetermining the free cause to this or that.

If any arguments seem to overthrow that knowledge, for instance that it cannot be grasped how God infallibly knows something to be future that could fail to be, those arguments also conflict with the foreknowledge of contingents that are absolutely future, and God's word puts it beyond all doubt that God has that foreknowledge.

source_text: LXIV. Sed certe tantum de nobis praesumere non debemus, ut divinam scientiam limitare ausimus, & negare quod Deus aliquid sciat, quia quomodo sciret comprehendere non valemus. Nam divinus intellectus omnimodo infinitus plus scit proculdubio quam valeamus capere & assequi. Saltem ille minus periculose errat, qui putat Deum scire ea quae forte scibilia non sunt; quam qui negat Deum scire quae revera scit, & quae intra divinae omniscientiae objectum continentur.
english: We certainly ought not to presume so much on ourselves as to dare to set limits to God's knowledge and deny that he knows something because we cannot understand how he would know it. God's intellect, infinite in every way, doubtless knows more than we can grasp or reach.

At any rate, someone who thinks God knows things that perhaps are not knowable errs less dangerously than someone who denies that God knows what he really does know, things that fall within the object of his omniscience.

source_text: LXV. Addo scientiam illam futurorum conditionate, qualem hactenus descripsimus, nullam necessariam connexionem habere cum erroribus variis, ad quos tuendos atque incrustandos plurimi ea abutuntur. Praesertim vero pertendimus illam nullo modo pugnare cum gratia per se efficaci, neque necesse esse ut illam adhibeamus ad conciliandam divinae gratiae efficaciam cum arbitrii humani libertate. Ut in sequentibus, Deo favente, ostendemus.
english: I add that the knowledge of conditional futures, as described so far, has no necessary connection with the various errors that very many misuse it to defend and gloss over.

Above all, we maintain that it in no way conflicts with grace that is efficacious of itself, and that we do not need it to reconcile the efficacy of God's grace with the freedom of human choice. With God's help, we will show this in what follows.
